summary: Describes the Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support protocol, which lets an entire mobile network attach to different points in the Internet. It extends Mobile IPv6 so that every node in the moving network keeps its sessions and stays reachable, with a Mobile Router connecting the network to the outside.

plainLanguage.summary: NEMO Basic Support lets a whole IPv6 network move while its devices keep their addresses and connections. A Mobile Router tells its Home Agent where it is, and the Home Agent relays traffic through a tunnel.

questions: how does nemo basic support work
what is the mobile router flag in binding update
subtitle: How a moving IPv6 network stays reachable through a Mobile Router and its Home Agent.

tldr.problem: When a whole network moves, its nodes need to keep their sessions and remain reachable without changing how they operate. Mobile IPv6 alone describes movement of a host, not the network behind a router.
tldr.mechanism: NEMO Basic Support extends Mobile IPv6. A Mobile Router registers its current Care-of Address and network prefixes with a Home Agent, which forwards traffic through a bidirectional tunnel.
tldr.outcome: Movement is hidden from nodes inside the Mobile Network, but their traffic passes through the Home Agent and the RFC does not define route optimization. RFC 3963 is a Proposed Standard; the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 3963 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Support Mobility for a Whole Network
sections.content:
RFC 3963 extends Mobile IPv6 so that an entire Mobile Network can attach at different points in the Internet. The network may contain devices that support mobility and devices that do not. Its movement should not require those devices to change their behavior.

A Mobile Router connects the moving network to the Internet and registers with a Home Agent. The RFC sends traffic between the Mobile Network and other nodes through that Home Agent; it does not define route optimization. Nested Mobile Routers are allowed, but each level adds an IPv6 header to data packets. Multihoming is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The devices inside a moving network can keep using it as their IPv6 network. A Mobile Router and Home Agent handle the movement, with the cost that traffic passes through the Home Agent.

sections.title: The Mobile Router and Home Agent
sections.content:
A Mobile Network is a subnet that can attach at different places in the routing infrastructure. It is reached through one or more Mobile Routers, which act as its gateways. A Mobile Router does not announce its network routes on the visited network; instead, it maintains a bidirectional tunnel to its Home Agent.

When the router moves, it obtains a Care-of Address on the visited link and sends a Binding Update to the Home Agent. The update's new R flag indicates that the sender is acting as a Mobile Router. A successful Binding Acknowledgement with R set tells it that the Home Agent has arranged forwarding for the Mobile Network.
sections.plainLanguage: The Mobile Router tells its Home Agent its new network address after moving. The Home Agent then knows where to send packets for the network behind that router.

sections.title: The Prefix Option and New Status Values
sections.content:
A Mobile Router can name the IPv6 prefixes it serves in a Mobile Network Prefix Option carried by a Binding Update. It may include multiple options when it wants forwarding for multiple prefixes. The option has type 6, length 18, a reserved byte, a prefix-length byte and a sixteen-byte prefix.

The Home Agent acknowledges the update with a status. RFC 3963 defines status values 140 through 143 for Mobile Router operation not permitted, invalid prefix, unauthorized prefix and forwarding setup failure. In implicit mode, the router sends no prefix option and the Home Agent relies on information configured by another means.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can list its network prefixes in its registration, or rely on the Home Agent to already know them. The reply reports whether the Home Agent accepted the request and set up forwarding.

sections.title: Registering and Forwarding Packets
sections.content:
A Mobile Router must support at least one of two registration modes. In explicit mode it includes Mobile Network Prefix Options in each relevant Binding Update, including refreshes. In implicit mode it sends no prefix options and the Home Agent uses preconfigured information. The R flag requires the Home Registration flag H to be set as well.

After a successful registration, packets from the Mobile Network are reverse-tunneled to the Home Agent using IP-in-IP encapsulation. The Home Agent removes the outer header and forwards them to their destination. In the other direction, the Home Agent tunnels packets for the Mobile Network to the router's Care-of Address, and the router forwards them inside its network.

If a Mobile Router returns to its home link, it deregisters. For a large Mobile Network, the router and Home Agent may optionally run an intra-domain routing protocol through the tunnel instead of listing prefixes in Binding Updates.
sections.plainLanguage: After registration, packets in both directions travel through the tunnel between the Mobile Router and Home Agent. The router removes or adds the tunnel header as needed, then forwards packets to their next destination.

sections.title: Optional Routing Through the Tunnel
sections.content:
The Mobile Router and Home Agent may run an intra-domain routing protocol, such as RIPng or OSPF, over the bidirectional tunnel. This option is controlled by configuration and can carry changing routes for a Mobile Network with multiple subnets.

When away from home, the Mobile Router should stop sending routing updates on its visited-link interface to reduce the chance of exposing Mobile Network prefixes there. The RFC requires authentication and confidentiality for routing messages from the Home Agent because those messages may reveal internal network structure. Link-state protocols also have tunnel-interface and OSPF-area guidance in Appendix B.
sections.plainLanguage: A large moving network can exchange route updates with its Home Agent through the tunnel. The router should keep those updates off the visited network and protect them because they may reveal internal routes.

sections.title: Protecting Signaling and Tunnel Traffic
sections.content:
Signaling between a Mobile Router and its Home Agent must be authenticated with IPsec, following the Mobile IPv6 protection rules. A Mobile Router should filter packets from its network so their source addresses belong to the Mobile Network Prefix and are not addresses used by the router itself.

The Home Agent must check tunneled packets: the outer source must be the Mobile Router's current Care-of Address, and the inner source must be valid for the Mobile Network prefixes. Before enabling forwarding for prefix options, the Home Agent must verify that the Mobile Router is authorized to use those prefixes. IPsec ESP can also protect tunneled payload packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The Home Agent and Mobile Router must authenticate their control messages. Both ends also check packet addresses so the tunnel cannot be used to send traffic with false source addresses.
